sources.title: U.S. National Park Service, Big Cypress National Preserve: Big Cypress Glades-period camps
sources.note: Big Cypress Glades-period camps, flooding, diet, food processing, shell/bone/fiber technology, limited farming, later decline. Carefully scope every claim to Big Cypress. The brochure explicitly says much remains mysterious and scant written records survive; it is useful for both daily life and uncertainty.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service, Biscayne National Park: Early Glades settlement
sources.note: Early Glades settlement, shell middens, pottery, sea-based subsistence, Miami River village and later Tequesta framing. Use for southeast-coast evidence, not as a full Glades-area generalization. Its later Tequesta language belongs to the contact-era identity discussion.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service, Southeast Archeological Center: Long-used hunting/fishing place
sources.note: Long-used hunting/fishing place, bone and wood preservation, fishing gear, site-function inference. Supports the distinction between a task site and a residential village. Dates span several millennia, so attach only dated or broad long-duration observations to the atlas interval.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service, Southeast Archeological Center: Bone and antler selection
sources.note: Bone and antler selection, manufacture, wooden hafts, use-wear and hunting. Good technology detail and gentle-fun-fact material: raccoon leg bones became carefully hafted points. Avoid assigning the work to a named gender or age group.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service, Southeast Archeological Center: Composite hooks
sources.note: Composite hooks, gorges, leisters, nets and weirs in Everglades fishing. Supports concrete daily-life mechanics. The observation that many gorges could fish while people did other work is a defensible lighthearted detail.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service, South Florida Collections: Glades Plain pottery chronology
sources.note: Glades Plain pottery chronology, cooking soot and later Glades Tooled bowls. Supports the 2,500-year start and the fact that soot, rather than an ancient calendar, can date cooking pottery. Keep the Anhinga dates site-specific.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service, Southeast Archeological Center: Wet-site preservation
sources.note: Wet-site preservation, possible pine structure pole, mahogany and other wooden shafts. Useful for explaining why wooden houses, containers and tools are undercounted archaeologically. The possible pole is an interpretation, not proof of a particular building.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service, Southeast Archeological Center: Animal species selected for bone tools and limits of zooarchaeological inference
sources.note: Animal species selected for bone tools and limits of zooarchaeological inference. Supports species-specific craft choices without claiming that every Glades community made identical tools.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service, Southeast Archeological Center: Plant-remain methods and local pine/mahogany identifications at Anhinga Trail
sources.note: Plant-remain methods and local pine/mahogany identifications at Anhinga Trail. Good evidence for local plant materials and for the medicine caveat: archaeobotany can identify wood or seeds, but species presence alone does not establish a medicinal recipe.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service: Tree-island daily-activity bases
sources.note: Tree-island daily-activity bases, wet preservation, sea-level erosion of Glades sites. Supports evidence-loss and preservation cautions. It is modern site stewardship, not evidence that ancient communities experienced today's climate trajectory.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service: Miami Circle architecture
sources.note: Miami Circle architecture, cut-hole pattern, black-earth midden and exchange questions. Use the cautious NPS phrasing: a probable structure footprint whose precise function remains unsettled. Do not label it a temple, council house or home as fact.

sources.title: Florida Division of Historical Resources: Official gateway to Miami Circle artifact studies
sources.note: Official gateway to Miami Circle artifact studies. Overview citation for the assemblage; prefer the individual study pages below for claims about chronology, diet or technology.

sources.title: Florida Division of Historical Resources: More than 500 bone/tooth objects; weaving
sources.note: More than 500 bone/tooth objects; weaving, hide processing, woodworking and bone working. Excellent exact-interval daily-life evidence, though the page does not identify maker gender, household organization or how children learned the skills.

sources.title: Florida Division of Historical Resources: Glades I-III ceramic sequence
sources.note: Glades I-III ceramic sequence, plain bowls, decorated wares and neighboring pottery. Primary chronology source: Glades I early is 500 BCE-CE 500. Use pottery as a dating category, not proof of one ethnic or political identity.

sources.title: Florida Division of Historical Resources: Radiocarbon series placing primary Miami Circle deposits about 750 BCE-CE 550
sources.note: Radiocarbon series placing primary Miami Circle deposits about 750 BCE-CE 550. Anchor for the atlas interval. It also shows a large later occupational break, warning against narrating uninterrupted site use.

sources.title: Florida Division of Historical Resources: Conch woodworking wedges
sources.note: Conch woodworking wedges, gouges/adzes, canoe/bowl manufacture and activity area. Strong technology and daily-work source. Canoe carving is a probable interpretation from context and tools, so retain 'likely' language.

sources.title: Florida Division of Historical Resources: Fish
sources.note: Fish, shark, ray, turtles and other foods; habitats; capture methods and canoe transport. Best exact-interval food source. Keep 'popular foods' and probable capture methods tied to the Miami Circle assemblage, not every Glades site.

sources.title: Florida Division of Historical Resources, Florida Master Site File: Current state archaeological period vocabulary and recording categories
sources.note: Current state archaeological period vocabulary and recording categories. Corroborates that Glades/Glades I are administrative archaeological classifications; use cautiously because its broad date entries differ from some refined local sequences.

sources.title: Miami-Dade County Historic Preservation: Later Glades mound
sources.note: Later Glades mound, river travel, mortuary questions, health/status research potential. A later-phase source. It describes what the unexcavated mound may reveal; do not report the listed health, mortality or status questions as established results.

sources.title: Miami-Dade County Parks: Key Biscayne settlement and post molds possibly outlining thatched houses
sources.note: Key Biscayne settlement and post molds possibly outlining thatched houses. Supports cautious house-form discussion near the atlas interval. The molds 'may indicate' house size and plan; do not turn that into a universal Glades home.

sources.title: Monroe County cultural-resource assessment: Florida Keys Glades chronology
sources.note: Florida Keys Glades chronology, ceramic markers, mounds, trade and contact-era transition. Regional professional report useful for later phases and chronology disagreements. Its social-stratification interpretation should be presented as archaeological inference.

sources.title: Florida International University Digital Commons / Dade County study: Environmental change
sources.note: Environmental change, Glades tradition definition, specialized subsistence zones, settlement and mortuary discussion. Broad local synthesis. Useful for ecology and research history; identify older interpretations and avoid treating all later Tequesta observations as Glades I facts.

sources.title: University of South Florida doctoral repository: Miami One demography
sources.note: Miami One demography, juvenile remains, infection, trauma, dental health and mortuary treatment. Best health/family evidence-limit source. It can show adults and juveniles in a community and skeletal stress, but not household kinship, parenting, healers or treatments.

sources.title: University of South Florida doctoral repository: Later Glades village seasonality and regional-center/hinterland models in the Florida Keys
sources.note: Later Glades village seasonality and regional-center/hinterland models in the Florida Keys. Use only in an after-500/later-phases box. It explicitly calls later Glades peoples understudied and models sociopolitical organization rather than proving it.

sources.title: Florida Museum of Natural History: Curated Glades
sources.note: Curated Glades, Belle Glade and Goodland pottery type collection. Shows material diversity and neighboring series. Do not imply that a pottery series maps neatly onto a tribe or language.

sources.title: Florida Museum of Natural History Ceramic Technology Laboratory: Glades Plain identification
sources.note: Glades Plain identification, period and regional occurrence. Concise material anchor. Note that the page's series/affiliation metadata reflects ceramic typology, not an ancient self-identification.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian: Key Marco wooden and tree-pitch object cataloged as possibly Glades and broadly dated CE 1-850
sources.note: Key Marco wooden and tree-pitch object cataloged as possibly Glades and broadly dated CE 1-850. Rare organic-technology evidence overlapping the atlas interval. Retain every catalog qualifier: it is a fragment, its function is cataloged under hunting/fishing/warfare, the cultural attribution is only 'possibly Glades,' and the date range extends beyond CE 500.

sources.title: Florida Museum of Natural History: Palm-fiber fishing net and anaerobic preservation at Key Marco
sources.note: Palm-fiber fishing net and anaerobic preservation at Key Marco, CE 700-1500. Later-phase technology only. It vividly explains why fiber rarely survives and why absence of cloth, baskets or nets in dry sites is not proof of absence in life.

sources.title: Florida Museum of Natural History Environmental Archaeology: Soil chemistry and texture methods for settlement boundaries
sources.note: Soil chemistry and texture methods for settlement boundaries, site use and post-depositional change. Evidence-method source for explaining what archaeology can detect. It does not by itself establish a particular Glades household or sanitation practice.

sources.title: Florida Museum of Natural History: South Florida environments
sources.note: South Florida environments, wet-site preservation and interpretation of perishable artifacts. Supports an accessible explanation for kids of why wet muck can save wood and fiber while ordinary sites erase them.

sources.title: University Press of Florida, John W. Griffin, Archaeology of the Everglades: Glades settlement typology
sources.note: Glades settlement typology, shell works, middens, beaches, mangrove-zone earth middens and site chronology. Foundational synthesis. Cite specific site-type observations; do not imply that later site distributions describe every century of the atlas interval.

sources.title: University Press of Florida / Oxford Academic: Reassessment rejecting direct or sustained Cuba-Glades contact from pottery resemblance
sources.note: Reassessment rejecting direct or sustained Cuba-Glades contact from pottery resemblance. Important myth-check. It supports restraint about overseas migration and shows why visual similarity alone is weak evidence.

sources.title: Smithsonian Institution, Gordon R. Willey: Foundational Gulf Coast archaeology and Glades material comparisons
sources.note: Foundational Gulf Coast archaeology and Glades material comparisons. Primary history-of-archaeology source. Prefer newer chronologies when they disagree and avoid repeating outdated ethnic equations without comment.

sources.title: University of Florida Digital Collections, John M. Goggin: Revised temporal chart and development of Florida archaeological chronology
sources.note: Revised temporal chart and development of Florida archaeological chronology. Primary historiographic source for the constructed nature of period labels. Use current DHR/NPS dates for the public-facing chronology.

sources.title: University of Florida educational resource: States that the later Tequesta language was never recorded
sources.note: States that the later Tequesta language was never recorded. Supports explicit absence, not a sample: no securely attested written Glades-language text exists for 500 BCE-CE 500. Explain that later Tequesta is only one contact-era population associated with part of the Glades area.

sources.title: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration: Records guide noting no federal-government record set for Tequesta and later naming variants
sources.note: Records guide noting no federal-government record set for Tequesta and later naming variants. Corroborates documentary scarcity and contact-era naming. It cannot prove that no record exists in Spanish archives.

sources.title: Seminole Tribe of Florida: Tribal account of deep Florida ancestry
sources.note: Tribal account of deep Florida ancestry, gathering of peoples, survival and present sovereignty. Use as a living sovereign nation's own account. Do not collapse the archaeological label 'Glades' into 'Seminole' or use archaeology to police the Tribe's ancestry.

sources.title: Seminole Tribe of Florida, Department of Anthropology and Genealogy: Tribal account of the Seminole people's complex formation
sources.note: Tribal account of the Seminole people's complex formation, distinctions among present sovereign nations and surviving Maskoki languages. Use as a sovereign tribal self-account showing that historical identity is layered and politically specific. Its modern language examples are not Glades-period samples and must never be retrojected to 500 BCE-CE 500.

sources.title: U.S. National Park Service and Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida: Present co-stewardship and Miccosukee oral-history connection to south Florida
sources.note: Present co-stewardship and Miccosukee oral-history connection to south Florida. Use for living homeland stewardship, with the agreement's own wording. Keep modern sovereignty distinct from an archaeological culture polygon.

sources.title: National Park Service, Archaeological Resources of Everglades National Park
sources.note: National Register documentation checked for the constructed Glades chronology, diagnostic pottery, Glades I dates, archaeological research history, regional evidence, and the sequence continuing beyond 500 CE.
